title: Different hands, same prayer
hookLine: schools differ on hand placement and small details, and all are valid within the tradition
last: RAK'AH — TWO, FOUR, FOUR, THREE, FOUR.

lines: HANDS LOW, HANDS HIGH, ARMS DOWN.
THEY BOW AT THE SAME MOMENT.
cards: Stand at the back of a big mosque during Friday prayer and look down the line. The man on the left has his hands folded low, below the navel. The one next to him, higher, on the chest.
The one next to him has his arms hanging straight at his sides. At the end of the Fatiha, some say amin out loud; some whisper it. A newcomer might think half the room is doing it wrong.
Nobody in the line thinks so. They're shoulder to shoulder, and they bow at the same moment.

teach.b: The word is madhhab, a school of law. Literally it means a way of going, the road someone takes.
In Islam's first centuries, scholars in different cities worked out how to follow the Qur'an and the Prophet's ﷺ example in daily life, and the ones whose methods lasted became schools.

teach.h: FOUR SUNNI SCHOOLS, AND THE JA'FARI.
teach.b: Among Sunni Muslims there are four, each named after a scholar: Abu Hanifa in Iraq, Malik in Medina, al-Shafi'i, and Ahmad ibn Hanbal. Twelver Shia Muslims follow the Ja'fari school, named after Ja'far al-Sadiq.
Why differ on something as simple as hands?
Because the reports differ. Companions saw the Prophet pray over years, in different places, and remembered different details.

So the Hanafi school commonly teaches hands folded below the navel; the Shafi'i, above the navel, below the chest; the Maliki school is known for leaving the arms at the sides, and so is Ja'fari practice.
Each has its reasons, going back to a report. There's a well-known story about Imam Malik. A caliph, the story goes, wanted to make Malik's book, the Muwatta, the law for the whole empire.
Malik said no. The companions, he said, had spread out to different lands, and each land had its own knowledge from them. Leave people with what they have.
People sometimes quote a saying, the differing of my community is a mercy; scholars note it isn't a reliable hadith.
But the attitude holds: within the tradition, all four Sunni schools are considered valid, and a Muslim can pray behind someone of another school.

teach.h: THE DETAILS DIFFER. THE PRAYER IS ONE.
teach.b: The details differ. The prayer is one.

how: A Muslim usually prays according to one school of law, often the one of their family or region, and pray side by side in the mosque with people who hold their hands, say amin or raise their hands a little differently.

practice: Picture the line in that mosque, or watch a short video of a prayer, and look at the hands: low, high, at the sides. If something in you wants to decide who's right, let it go.
Then stand and try each for one breath, hands low, hands high, arms hanging, and notice the prayer doesn't change; if you pray, you already know your own way, so just hold it gently.

wordCard.voice: Madhhab. A school of Islamic law, a way of going; four Sunni schools and the Ja'fari, one prayer. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: a school of law; literally, a way of going, a road taken.

carryVoice: Your line: many hands, one prayer. Shoulder to shoulder, the line still bows together. That's one hundred ten.
